They also held that it is completely internal and does not depend on spoken language. As al-Shahrastānī said in the passage above, a person may “take up a pen and write an entire volume from the conversation of his thought, filling a book with the conversation of his self, while his tongue remains silent and says nothing.”
On this basis, the Muʿtazilites concluded that inner speech is the feature that most clearly distinguishes human beings from animals.
In other words, it is the basic quality that makes a human being human.
Here they differ from the logicians, who defined the human being as a speaking animal.

The Muʿtazilite definition would instead amount to something like this: the human being is a rational animal, a thinking animal, or an animal that speaks through thought—that is, through the silent inner speech of the mind rather than through words spoken by the tongue.

“the way spoken expressions point to meaning differs from one nation and age to another, while the way judgments [that is, judgments of reason] point to knowledge is the way of reason itself, and this does not differ between nations and ages.”
Different words can therefore point to the same meaning.
The meaning understood when you say “God” is the same meaning understood from words such as Khudā, Tamkri, Sarnā, Nad, and so on.

The speech within the human self is therefore genuine speech and real expression. For the Muʿtazilites, it is the most distinctive quality of the human self and the feature that separates human beings from other animals.

“The inner conversations of the self are representations of the expressions spoken by the tongue. Do you not see that a person who does not know a word of Arabic does not have Arabic speech occur in his mind, and a person who does not know a foreign language does not have the speech of that language occur in his mind? But someone who knows both languages will sometimes speak inwardly to himself in Arabic and sometimes in the other language. Know, then, that in truth these are representations that follow the expressions a person learned while growing up. Yet the expressions themselves have those representations as their source: from them the expressions emerge, and back to them they return.”

As we see it, this argument in all its detail rests on the Muʿtazilite belief that the intellectual meaning or content remains one, even when the words used to express it differ from one people to another and from one language to another.
This is why they said that

“speech is not a kind of attribute with an independent rational reality like other attributes. Rather, the term is applied to speech by the tongue because people have agreed among themselves to use it in this way.”

A human being can be in a state in which neither speech nor its opposite is present, while still remaining fully human. A person is therefore distinguished from animals by his form and structure, not by spoken speech.
Spoken language, then, is not something that has an independent rational reality of its own. It consists of terms and expressions that people agree among themselves to use.
And a human being can at times be silent—neither speaking nor doing the opposite of speaking—without ceasing to be human.
So spoken language cannot be what fundamentally distinguishes human beings from animals.
What distinguishes them instead is their form and structure.

Here, “form” is meant in the Aristotelian sense. The point is that matter itself is not what distinguishes the human being. What does so is the particular form that makes a human being human and separates the human kind from the other kinds of beings in the external world.
In short, for the Muʿtazilites, rational reality is the basic feature that distinguishes human beings from animals.
If we look more closely at the Muʿtazilite explanation of language and of the relationship between language and thought, we can see a limitation in their view.
Given the period in which they lived, they were unable to recognize that language and thought cannot truly be separated, even in the silent inner speech that is never spoken aloud.
But their account also contains something else that was highly progressive in relation to the ideas about language common in their own society and age.
As we have seen, they argued that language comes into existence through agreement among people. Human beings themselves create it.
Today this may seem completely obvious. So what was important about the Muʿtazilites saying something that now appears so self-evident?
The answer is that it was not self-evident in their own time or in the intellectual world in which they lived.
The idea that language came from divine revelation was widespread.
Against this, the Muʿtazilites argued that language comes from people themselves, who agree on words in order to express meanings. In its own time, this was an advanced position.
They also gave this view another theoretical basis beyond the arguments we have just examined.
Their second argument was that language is something that came into being in time and is material. The proof, they said, is that languages differ from one people to another.
If language were eternal, it would be fixed and there would be a single language shared by all peoples.
This theoretical principle became one of the foundations of the Muʿtazilite doctrine of the created Qurʾān.
6 — The Question of Rational Good and Evil
This question also grew out of the Muʿtazilite principle of divine justice, and especially from their belief that human freedom of choice is essential to any meaningful idea of justice.
The Muʿtazilites agreed that reason alone can recognize that the world has a Creator, and that reason can distinguish good from evil.

They also held that because God is just, He requires of human beings only what they are genuinely free to choose to do. That freedom rests on the reason God has given them, because reason is the faculty through which choice becomes possible.
From this it followed that they had to accept a position such as Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf’s:

A morally responsible human being must know that what is good is good and what is evil is evil. He must therefore do what is good, such as truthfulness and justice, and turn away from what is evil, such as lying and injustice.
The same idea appears in al-Naẓẓām and others, who held that reason itself judges all human actions to be good or bad.
It also appears in al-Jubbāʾī and his son Abū Hāshim ʿAbd al-Salām, who argued that knowing what is good and what is evil is itself a rational obligation.

Statements like these, found across the writings of different Muʿtazilite thinkers, all belong to the issue that became known during this rich period in the development of Arab-Islamic thought as “the question of rational good and evil.”
We saw earlier, when discussing Jahm ibn Ṣafwān, that he was the first to think seriously about this issue and to give its theoretical basis an early form.
The Muʿtazilites then developed it further until it took on the philosophical form associated with the theologians of kalām.
Its basic meaning, however, remained what Jahm had first proposed: reason by itself can discover whether things and actions are good or bad, beneficial or harmful.
On this basis, Jahm and, after him, the Muʿtazilites argued that “reason makes knowledge obligatory before revelation is heard.”

That is, reason obliges a morally responsible person to know God and to know the basic principles of religious law even before hearing what is taught by prophets, messengers, or books of divine revelation.

When discussing this question in relation to Jahm, we said that at first sight it might appear to have only one side: a metaphysical purpose and content, since the knowledge said to be required by reason includes knowledge of God and of the basic principles of divine law.
But we should not overlook another side of the issue, which is implied rather than stated directly.
This second side has two rationalist aspects.
First, it recognizes that reason can reach knowledge on its own, without the mediation of revealed law. In this sense, reason has an independent role in acquiring knowledge.
Second, it recognizes that good and evil exist objectively in things and actions themselves.
And this, in turn, implies that the things themselves also exist objectively.
There is, however, a major difference between the way this question appears in Jahm and the way it appears among the Muʿtazilites.
The difference lies in their way of thinking.
Jahm contradicted his own deterministic method when he accepted the idea of rational good and evil.

The Muʿtazilites, by contrast, remained completely consistent with their own coherent system. They based this question on their doctrine of human freedom of choice, which in turn rested on the human faculty of reason.
Abū al-Hudhayl comes close to saying this openly in the passage quoted above:
“He must therefore do what is good, such as truthfulness and justice, and turn away from what is evil, such as lying and injustice.”
For Abū al-Hudhayl, doing and turning away are human actions performed because reason itself requires them.
Here, “requirement” means an inner and voluntary motive guided by reason.
The same applies to al-Naẓẓām’s statement that reason judges actions good or bad in everything a person does.
His judgment of good and evil is directly connected to human conduct, and the motive comes from the person’s own reason.
This is why the question remained somewhat isolated and abstract in Jahm’s thought, while among the Muʿtazilites it became closely connected with the other parts of their theory of divine justice.
Above all, it was connected with the central part of that theory: human freedom of choice.

This idea makes the theory as a whole into a bridge between the concept of divine justice and the practical responsibility of human beings—not only in the moral sphere, but in the social sphere as well.
There is another side to the Muʿtazilite development of this question: they placed it on a rational and argumentative foundation.

By doing so, they gave the issue a new theoretical form and prepared the way for it to become part of the first Arab-Islamic philosophical system to take on the character of an organized science: the science of kalām.
The Muʿtazilites offered several arguments for their belief that reason can judge good and evil. We will mention three of them here.
The first is based on historical observation and an inductive method.

They argue that before revealed laws appeared, people already used reason to settle disputes. They argued with one another rationally, and each side tried to bind its opponent by what reason itself required.
This was possible only because people appealed to what reason could recognize as good or evil in things themselves, independently of any revealed law—since no revealed law yet existed.
For example, rational people before the coming of religious laws regarded saving a drowning person or rescuing someone from destruction as good. They regarded oppression and aggression as bad.
Their second argument works through logical necessity.
The prophets, they say, ask people to use their reason and reflect on the things in the universe.
But suppose things were not good or bad in themselves, and suppose reason could not recognize their qualities without first depending on revelation.
People could then say to the prophets:

We are not required to examine your miracles or your claims to prophethood unless revelation first tells us to do so. But revelation itself cannot be established unless we first examine your prophethood and your miracles.
The prophets would then have no answer, and their whole mission would collapse.
But that conclusion is false, the Muʿtazilites argue.
So the logical problem is resolved only if things really can be good or bad in themselves, and if reason can recognize this before revealed law arrives.

Their third argument is that if actions were not good or bad in themselves, and received these qualities only from revealed law, then legal scholars would be unable to use reason in cases where no scriptural ruling exists.
It would also become impossible to explain why a particular rule exists.
The question “Why?” and the answer “Because…” would lose their meaning, because every explanation depends on the assumption that things and actions possess real qualities of their own.
Aḥmad Amīn sums up what the Muʿtazilite position truly means:

“The Muʿtazilites affirmed the authority of reason in knowing good and evil. Good is not good merely because God imposed it on things, nor is evil evil for that reason. To put it differently, God’s command does not make a thing good, and His prohibition does not make it evil. Rather, God commands a thing because it is good in itself, and prohibits it because it is evil in itself. Things possess qualities in their own nature that make them good or evil, and reason is capable of recognizing these qualities and thereby knowing good and evil. There is no doubt that this principle frees reason from rigidity and from stopping at the literal text…”
To understand the historical and intellectual place of the Muʿtazilite position more clearly, we need to compare it with the Ashʿarite view.
Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī, the founder of the Ashʿarite school, says:
“Reason makes nothing obligatory, nor does it judge anything to be good or evil. Knowledge of God is reached through reason, but it becomes obligatory through revelation.”
